row.name: Fort Abbas
row.description: The region of Fort Abbas is associated with the ancient Ghaggar Hakra river system, which is believed by many scholars to represent a former river course linked to early urban settlements in South Asia [1]. Archaeological investigations in the Cholistan Desert have recorded hundreds of ancient settlement sites along the dry riverbed [1]. Surveys conducted by early researchers and later archaeologists documented continuous human occupation dating back to the fourth millennium BCE [1]. The earliest cultural material discovered in the region is known as Hakra Ware [1]. Before the modern name Fort Abbas was adopted, the settlement was known as Pholra [1]. It functioned as a fortified outpost along caravan trade routes connecting Multan with regions of present day Rajasthan and northern India [1]. The settlement played an important role in protecting trade routes across the Cholistan Desert [1].

row.name: Derby Racecourse Roman Settlement
row.description: The Derby Racecourse Roman settlement was the third settlement in Derby or Derventio which was a small town in the Roman province of Britannia [1]. It lies 600m east of Derventio fort in Little Chester, on the outskirts of Derby [1]. The Roman road from Derventio to Sawley on the River Trent passes the settlement [1]. Derby Racecourse Roman settlement site was founded around AD 90 [1]. The site was excavated between 1968 and 1983 [1].

row.name: Dobberworth
row.description: The Dobberworth or Dubberworth is one of the largest prehistoric tumuli in northern Germany, located on the isle of Rügen near Sagard [1]. The Dubberworth is about 15 metres tall, and was made from an estimated 22,000 cubic metres of earth, making it the largest tumulus in Rügen [1]. Archaeologists have not been able to date the tumulus precisely, but assume it was used during the Bronze Age [1]. According to local legends, the Dubberworth was made by a giant who intended to fill a narrow ford linking two nearby Bodden and lost the clay on their way [1].

row.name: Pavlopetri
row.description: Pavlopetri is an archaeologial site in Vatika Bay, off the coast of southern Laconia in Peloponnese, Greece [1]. Pavlopetri is unique in having an almost complete town plan, including streets, buildings, and tombs [1]. The existence of submerged walls at the site was first noted in 1904 by the geologist Fokion Negris but little was reported of their extent or state of preservation [1]. Originally, the ruins were dated to the Mycenaean period, 1600–1100 BCE but later studies showed a much earlier occupation dating back to 3500 BCE, so it also includes artifacts from the Final Neolithic Age, Chalcolithic Age, Bronze Age, and middle Minoan and transitional material [1]. It is now believed that the town was submerged around 1000 BCE by the first of three earthquakes that the area suffered [1]. The city has at least 15 buildings submerged in 3 to 4 metres of water [1].

row.name: Pikestones
row.description: Pikestones is the remains of a Neolithic Burial Cairn, located on Anglezarke moor in Lancashire [1]. The site is approximately 150 feet long and 60 feet across at its widest point [1]. It consisted of one burial chamber constructed of large upright slabs, capped by two lintel slabs, forming a chamber of 15 feet long, 3 feet wide and 3 feet high, covered by a huge mound of stones and turves [1]. The cairn was aligned almost exactly North-South, with the burial chamber under the wider northern end [1]. Today the cairn has been badly robbed and the main features are the five large gritstone slabs, the remains of the burial chamber [1]. Pikestones is the earliest man-made structure in the area and only one other chambered tomb has been found in Lancashire [1]. The monument must have taken an immense amount of labour to construct and like most long barrows was erected in a prominent position, located on a ridge at a height of just over 900 feet [1].

row.name: Jisk'a Iru Muqu
row.description: Jisk'a Iru Muqu is a pre-Columbian open-air site in the Aymara community of Jachacachi, 54 km southeast of Puno, Peru, in the Lake Titicaca Basin [1]. Occupied from c. 3400-1600 BCE (Late Archaic to Early Formative), it was the first Archaic open-air site excavated in the Titicaca Basin, discovered by Mark Aldenderfer in 1994 [1] [2] [3]. Excavations recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace, and early domestic architecture showing reduced residential mobility [1] [4]. The site provides critical evidence for the transition from mobile foraging to settled village life in the south-central Andes [1] [5].

row.name: Roman Vaults of Nuncio Viejo
row.description: Located beneath Calle Nuncio Viejo, these Roman vaults consist of a system of walls and barrel vaults dating to the Roman era according to archaeological studies [1] [2]. They sit near two of the city's most important Roman remains: the Roman baths and cisterns of the water distribution network [3] [4]. Restored and enhanced by the Toledo Consortium by April 2008, they are now accessible to visitors through the "Unknown Heritage" (Patrimonio Desconocido) guided routes programme [1] [5] [6].

row.name: Alb Limes
row.description: The Alb Limes is a Roman frontier fortification or limes of the late 1st century AD in the Swabian Jura, also known as the Swabian Alb [1]. The Alb Limes runs for just under 135 kilometres from Rottweil (Latin: Arae Flaviae) in the southwest to Heidenheim an der Brenz (Latin: Aquileia), Germany, in the northeast [1].

row.name: Tell Maghzaliyah
row.description: Tell Maghzaliyah, in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq, is a prehistoric fortified aceramic Mesolithic and Neolithic site located approximately 7.5 km northwest of Yarim Tepe, with which it shows some similarities [1]. It is situated near the Abra River, a tributary of the Habur River, which eventually drains into the Euphrates River [1]. Tell Maghzaliyah shows the development of pre-Hassuna culture [1]. There are also numerous connections to the Jarmo culture going back to 7000 BCE [1]. The site is approximately 4500 square meters in area, and the depth of deposit is approximately 8 meters [1]. It was excavated during 12 seasons between 1969 and 1980 on the Sinjar Plain, by a Soviet team from the Institute of Archaeology [1].

row.name: Hampton Down Stone Circle
row.description: Positioned at the national grid reference 35960865, Hampton Down Stone Circle is located on the southern edge of an open downland ridge at a height of 680 feet above sea level [1]. A photograph from 1908 showed sixteen stones as part of the monument [1]. However, by 1964 twenty-eight stones were found to be part of the circle [1]. In 1964 the stones in the circle were disturbed by agricultural activity [1]. It was then decided that the site would be excavated, a project which was ordered by the Ministry of Public Building and Works and carried out in May 1965 under the directorship of Geoffrey J. Wainwright [1]. The excavation revealed that the location of the stones was not their original prehistoric position [1]. The original location of the circle was identified as existing a few feet to the west [1]. The original circle had either eight or possibly nine sockets for stones and was oval shaped [1].

row.name: Jenny's Lantern
row.description: Situated on the southern slope of the Jenny's Lantern area is an Iron Age hillfort [1]. The Jenny's Lantern area is a small south-facing hill or promontory rising to 144 metres above the Aln valley's 50 metres floor, 1.32 miles north-east of Bolton and 2.7 miles south of Eglingham, villages in north Northumberland [1]. Jenny's Lantern hillfort is an Iron Age defended settlement, undated, but falling within a style dating from circa 700BCE to 100CE [1]. Remains of at least 15 stone-founded circular huts of from 4 metres to 6 metres diameter are evident, three within the fort and the remainder in a series of seven embanked enclosures outside it [1]. A field system delineated by rubble and boulder boundaries is found to the south and east of the enclosures [1]. A lacrymatory was discovered at the site in 1824, and a quern-stone in 1885 [1].

row.name: Paglicci Cave
row.description: Paglicci Cave, near Rignano Garganico in Apulia, is one of Europe's most important Paleolithic sites, with a 12-metre stratigraphic sequence [1] [2]. Over 45,000 individual finds include lithic tools, bone points, and two Gravettian burials dating to around 30,000 years ago [1] [2] [3]. A pestle from approximately 32,000 BP preserved starch granules from wild oats [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Kingston Russell Stone Circle
row.description: Kingston Russell Stone Circle, also known as the Gorwell Circle, is a stone circle located between the villages of Abbotsbury and Littlebredy in the south-western English county of Dorset [1]. Archaeologists believe that it was likely erected during the Bronze Age [1]. The Kingston Russell ring is part of a tradition of stone circle construction that spread throughout much of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany during the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age, over a period between 3,300 and 900 BCE [1]. The site has not been excavated or been subject to in-depth archaeological investigation [1]. Kingston Russell is the largest surviving stone circle in Dorset [1]. The stones are arranged in an oval with a diameter measuring from 24 by 27 metres (79 by 89 feet) [1]. The ring consists of eighteen stones, the longest of which are located at the north of the circle [1]. As of 1939, all the stones were lying on the ground, although there is a record that in 1815 one stone on the southern side was still standing upright [1].

row.name: Stannon Stone Circle
row.description: Stannon stone circle (also known as Stannon circle or simply Stannon) is a stone circle located near St. Breward on Bodmin Moor in Cornwall, England [1]. The stones average size is around 0.5 metres with the largest stone in the group having a base width of over 1.2 metres [1]. Stannon is an example of Alexander Thom's Type A flattened circle, being noticeably flattened on the north side [1]. When standing in the supposed centre of Stannon Circle, a point between twenty-two and twenty-eight degrees north from east is marked by Rough Tor [1].

row.name: Mynydd Illtud
row.description: Mynydd Illtud is an extensive area of common land near Libanus, Powys, Wales, located in the Brecon Beacons National Park and some three miles south-west of Brecon [1]. The common is an undulating plateau lying between 330 and 370 metres above sea level [1]. Its highest points are 381 metres at Allt Lom and 367 metres at Twyn y Gaer trig point overlooking the valley of the River Usk [1]. Twyn y Gaer is the site of an Iron Age hill fort [1]. The Iron Age hillfort of Twyn y Gaer sits atop the grassy mound on the northern tip of the common [1]. Research by A. H. A. Hogg on this hill fort was published in 1982 [1]. The course of a Roman road, Sarn Helen can be traced from south-west to north-east across the common [1].

row.name: Anta da Pedra dos Mouros
row.description: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, also known as the Anta do Senhor da Serra, is a megalithic dolmen situated near Belas and Queluz in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. It is believed to date back to the late-Neolithic and early-Chalcolithic eras (4000-2500 BC) [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros, the Anta da Estria, and the Anta do Monte Abraão are a short distance from each other and are collectively known as the Antas de Belas [1]. The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner [1]. The burial chamber was at that time already in bad condition, having only three upright support stones, with one apparently having two anthropomorphic figures engraved on it [1]. Items found by Ribeiro during his excavations are kept in the Geological Museum in Lisbon [1]. They include a stone axe, flint tools, utensils for domestic use, vases, and human and animal bones [1].

row.name: Almsworthy Common
row.description: Almsworthy Common is an area of unenclosed moorland on Exmoor in southwestern England [1] [2]. The site features a multiple stone row of at least 29.8 m with 15 stones in four rows aligned roughly NW-SE, and is a Scheduled Monument [3] [4]. Stone settings are the most common megalithic monuments on Exmoor, likely serving ceremonial or ritual purposes [5] [6].

row.name: Castle Dore
row.description: Castle Dore — or Castle Dôr — is an Iron Age hill fort near Golant in Cornwall [1]. It was probably occupied from the 5th or 4th centuries BC until the 1st century BC [1]. The perimeter of Castle Dore consists of two ditches [1]. The inner ditch is circular, measuring 79 metres in diameter internally, and the outer ditch arced round it from the north to the south-east before widening in the north east to form an entrance [1]. Archaeologist Ralegh Radford led excavations at Castle Dore in 1936 and '37 [1]. At the time of Radford's work, archaeologists tended to concentrate on the defences in the course of examining hillforts; Radford, however, investigated the interior and found postholes belonging to huts of at least two distinct phases of occupation [1].

row.name: Anta do Monte Abraão
row.description: The Anta do Monte Abraão was a megalithic dolmen located in the parish of Monte Abraão, in Queluz, Sintra Municipality, Lisbon District [1]. The dolmen was first identified in 1876, by Carlos Ribeiro, who carried out excavations until 1878 and published his results in 1880 [1]. Excavations suggest that it served as a tomb for about 80 individuals and that it dates back to the middle to end of the Neolithic period (4000-2500 BC) [1]. The burial chamber of the Anta do Monte Abraão had an east-west orientation [1]. It had at least six upright limestone supporting stones or orthostats and three of these were found in situ by Ribeiro [1]. The polygonal chamber had a diameter of 3.6 metres, approached by an 8 metre corridor that was 2 metres wide [1]. Despite the destruction of the tomb, excavations have yielded numerous finds, including stone axes, flint tools and blades, flint arrowheads, club heads, pottery ceramics, clay vessels and objects of adornment [1]. These are exhibited at the Portuguese Geological Museum in Lisbon [1].

row.name: Shovel Down
row.description: Shovel Down is an area of Dartmoor in Devon that is covered in megaliths including the remains of several stone rows, the Fourfold Stone Circle, and several standing stones [1]. The Shovel Down stone row complex occupies the northern and southern slopes of a broad east-west ridge of unenclosed moorland [1]. It is of probable Bronze Age date [1]. Approximately five double stone rows and one single stone row are to be seen [1]. The Fourfold Circle is a configuration of four concentric stone circles [1]. The Fourfold Circle is the location of a turf-covered cairn with a central cist which has been robbed [1]. The Long Stone stands in the middle of two stone rows [1]. It is referred to as the "Langstone" in a documentary source of 1240 [1].

row.name: Hunnum
row.description: Hunnum (also known as Onnum, and with the modern name of Halton Chesters) was a Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall located north of the modern-day village of Halton, Northumberland in North East England [1]. It was the fifth fort on Hadrian's Wall and is situated about 7.5 miles west of Vindobala fort [1]. The site of the fort is bisected by the B6318 Military Road [1]. The original fort was built between 122 and 126 AD with a rectangular plan measuring 460 feet north to south by 410 feet east to west [1]. A dedicatory slab from the west gate of the fort tells us that the Legio VI Victrix were responsible for the initial building work [1]. The fort was initially garrisoned, probably, by a cohort of 500 partly mounted troops [1]. In the third century it held a regiment of cavalry transferred from Arbeia fort, the Ala I Pannoniorum Sabiniana, also called Ala Sabiniana [1]. The field north of the Military Road containing the northern section of the fort was first ploughed in 1827, and a fine bath-house was found [1].

row.name: Burnmoor Stone Circles
row.description: The Burnmoor Stone Circles are a group of five different approximately 4,000-year-old stone circles in Cumbria [1]. They are around 1 mile north of the village of Boot, on the slopes of Boat How [1]. The largest circle is known as Brat's Hill and there are two nearby pairs of circles known as White Moss and Low Longrigg [1]. Brat's Hill is the largest stone circle with around 42 stones forming an irregular circle with a diameter of 30 metres [1]. There are five funerary cairns within the circle together with two further stones [1]. About 100 metres to the northwest of Brat's Hill circle lie the two White Moss stone circles [1]. One of them measures 16 metres in diameter and has 11 stones forming the circle, while the other measures 16.5 metres in diameter and has 14 stones forming the circle [1]. Both stone circles have internal cairns [1].

row.name: Öküzlü Ören Yeri
row.description: Okuzlu Oren Yeri is an archaeological site in the Erdemli district of Mersin Province, Turkey [1]. The site was occupied during the Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine periods, featuring remains including a basilica structure from the Byzantine phase [1] [2]. Polygonal masonry characterizes the oldest surviving structures, while later constructions used smooth cut stone [2] [3].

row.name: Shilikty
row.description: Shilikty, formerly Chilikti, also more precisely Baigetobe Kurgans in Shilikty Valley, is an archaeological site in eastern Kazakhstan, located in the Chilik river basin [1]. At this site, numerous 8th-6th century BCE Early Saka kurgans were found [1]. Carbon-14 dating suggests a more refined date of 730-690 BCE for the kurgans, and a broad contemporaneity with the Arzhan-2 kurgan in Tuva [1]. The Kurgans contained vast quantities of precious golden jewelry [1]. Remains of a "golden man" were found in 2003, with 4262 gold finds [1].

row.name: Tomb of Macridy Bey
row.description: The Tomb of Macridy Bey, also known as the Tomb of Langadas, is an ancient Macedonian tomb of the Classical or early Hellenistic period, on the site of ancient Lete, modern Derveni between Thessaloniki and Langadas, in Central Macedonia [1]. A number of cist graves and a single chamber tomb are located in the vicinity [1]. The structure seems to date to the late fourth or early third century BCE [1]. The tomb consists of a monumental facade and two vaulted chambers (an antechamber and a burial chamber) on an east-west axis, covered by an extremely large earthen tumulus 19.5 m high and 76 m in diameter [1]. The 7.83 m high facade consists of four engaged Ionic columns [1]. The tomb had already been looted and suffered earthquake damage when it was discovered and excavated in 1910 by Theodore Makridi, from whom it takes its modern name [1].

row.name: Wayna Tawqaray
row.description: Wayna Tawqaray is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is located in the Cusco Region, Cusco Province, San Sebastián District, about 5 km southeast of the center of Cusco [1]. Wayna Tawqaray is situated at a height of about 3,600 metres on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray [1]. The mountain with the archaeological remains lies southeast of the mountain Araway Qhata and the hill Muyu Urqu, above the river Watanay [1].

row.name: Wicklewood Roman Temple
row.description: Wicklewood Roman Temple is the site of a Romano-Celtic temple near Wicklewood and about 1.5 miles north-west of Wymondham, in Norfolk [1]. The site was discovered in 1959 from cropmarks, and a partial excavation took place in August of that year [1]. The buried remains of a temple were found [1]. It was a rectangular building, about 15 metres north to south by 17 metres west to east [1]. There was a cella (an inner chamber), about 8.5 metres square, built of mortared flint rubble; internally the walls were plastered, and were painted with a design in yellow and black on a red ground [1]. The temple evidently served an adjacent settlement, as many Roman objects, such as pottery fragments, coins, brooches and figurines, dating from the first to fourth centuries A.D. have been found near the temple [1]. Some of the brooches are ornate, suggesting that they were votive offerings [1].

row.name: Rempstone Stone Circle
row.description: Rempstone Stone Circle is a stone circle near to Corfe Castle on the Isle of Purbeck in the south-western English county of Dorset [1]. Archaeologists believe that it was likely erected during the Bronze Age [1]. The southern half of the circle has been destroyed, with five upright and three recumbent stones remaining extant [1]. In 1957, a possible avenue of stones leading to the circle was discovered by ploughing but subsequently removed [1]. The incomplete stone circle lies in a dense wood just to the south of the B3351 road, 4 kilometres east of Corfe Castle and 5 kilometres west of Studland [1]. The stones are sandstone boulders which geologically belong to the Bagshot Beds, on which the circle is located [1].

row.name: Carnedd y Ddelw Cairn
row.description: Carnedd y Ddelw is a Bronze Age burial cairn in the Carneddau mountains of north Wales, occupying a summit northeast of Foel-fras [1]. The summit features two large shelter cairns hollowed from a massive prehistoric burial cairn [1] [2]. Its eastern slopes drain via Afon Tafolog to Afon Roe, flowing through Rowen before joining the River Conwy [1]. The site forms the final top on Carnedd Llewelyn's long northern spur, with Tal y Fan to the northeast [1] [3].

row.name: Cave of Pedra Furada
row.description: The Cave of Pedra Furada is a small cave located in the municipality of Vila Franca de Xira, about 20 km north of Lisbon in Portugal [1]. Archaeological studies conducted within the cave suggest it was occupied intermittently by humans during at least three periods between the end of the fourth millennium BC and the second millennium BC [1]. The cave results from karstification of the limestone Upper Jurassic Massif [1]. The first formal archaeological excavation was carried out in 1955 by a team led by Hipólito Cabaço [1]. This identified a communal funeral space, and radiocarbon dating of one individual's bones indicates that the use of the cave as a necropolis dates back to between 3095 BC and 2915 BC [1]. Archaeologists also collected a number of objects, such as bone drills, beads of various materials, flint arrowheads, microliths, a polished stone axe, fragments of pottery and a bone figurine of a rabbit [1].

row.name: Oppidum Uetliberg
row.description: Oppidum Uetliberg was a La Tene era Celtic fortification near the summit of Uetliberg hill in the canton of Zurich, Switzerland, dating to the 5th century BC (late Hallstatt/early La Tene period) [1]. One of the most important Iron Age fortifications in Switzerland, it featured walls up to 14m high and 35m wide enclosing a large settlement with two inner defensive rings [1]. The hilltop was settled from at least the Neolithic period, with the oldest artifacts dating to around 4000 BC among some 60,000 total finds [1]. Early excavations were conducted in the 1830s and 1860s [1].

row.name: Bokerley Dyke
row.description: Bokerley Dyke, Bokerly Dyke, Bokerley Ditch, is a linear earthwork 5.75 kilometres long on Cranborne Chase in Dorset, partially running along the county's border with Hampshire between Woodyates and Martin [1]. It is part of a Scheduled Monument together with Grim's Ditch and other associated earthworks [1]. Bokerley Dyke was excavated by Augustus Pitt Rivers between 1888 and 1891 and by Philip Rahtz in advance of road widening in 1958 [1]. Bokerley Dyke may have originated in the Bronze Age or Early Iron Age and formed a political and cultural boundary [1]. It was cut through by a Roman Road in the 1st century [1]. In the 4th century it was remodelled and brought back into use, and excavations show that the Roman road was blocked [1]. A coin of Valens dates this activity to shortly after 364 AD [1].

row.name: Le Regourdou
row.description: Le Regourdou is an archaeological site in the Dordogne department, France, on top of a hill just 800 m from the famous cave complex of Lascaux [1]. At this now collapsed 35 m deep ancient karst cavity remarkably well preserved Neanderthal fossils were recovered, that might be skeletal remains of deliberate burials [1]. The site of Regourdou was discovered by chance in 1954 by its owner, Roger Constant [1]. Apart from a Neanderthal skeleton discovered in 1957, excavator Eugène Bonifay found a large number of brown bear bones, several pits and stone platforms that contained bear bones [1].

row.name: Roman Bridge of Catribana
row.description: The Roman Bridge of Catribana is located near the village of Catribana in the parish of São João das Lampas, in the municipality of Sintra in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. The bridge, which crosses the Bolelas stream, is made of local limestone blocks [1]. It is likely to have provided access for a Roman villa to a main road or connected two important Roman villas at the time when the area was part of the Roman Olisipo, in the province of Lusitania, which formed part of the Roman Empire [1]. It is composed of a single arch and parapet, and has undergone several changes over the centuries [1]. On its south side is a section of a Roman path, about 50 meters long, which gives access to the bridge [1]. Close to the bridge archaeologists have identified vestiges of a Roman-era cemetery together with remains of a Neolithic settlement [1].

row.name: Three Brothers of Grugith
row.description: The Three Brothers of Grugith is a prehistoric site, a dolmen of the Neolithic Age, near St Keverne in Cornwall, England [1]. It is a scheduled monument [1]. The dolmen is situated near the summit of a hill overlooking Goonhilly Downs [1]. Two orthostats support a capstone; there are depressions on the capstone which may be cup marks, or may be naturally formed [1]. The chamber enclosed by the stones measures about 4 by 2 metres (13.1 by 6.6 ft), height about 1 metre (3 ft 3 in) [1]. William Copeland Borlase excavated the chamber in 1872: he discovered a pit about 1 metre (3 ft 3 in) deep, and one flint flake [1].

row.name: Showery Tor
row.description: Showery Tor is a rocky outcrop on a ridge-top approximately 0.6 kilometres north of the Rough Tor summit, near Camelford on Bodmin Moor in Cornwall [1]. It is notable for its rock formations and prehistoric monuments [1]. The site was thought to have been a religious focal point, possibly from the Neolithic or Bronze Age period [1]. No excavations have been recorded at the site, and it is not known if any burials were made there [1]. The granite outcrop is reminiscent of the Cheesewring and made of individual blocks on underlying outcrops formed by erosion along horizontal fractures in the granitic mass [1].

row.name: Tell Yunatsite
row.description: Tell Yunatsite, also known as Ploskata mogila, is situated in the Pazardzhik Province of southern Bulgaria, some 8 kilometres to the west of the district capital Pazardzhik [1]. The tell stands 12 metres above modern ground level and has a diameter of 110 m [1]. It is situated on a low terrace at the right bank of the former Topolnitsa riverbed near to its confluence with the Maritsa River (ca. 5 km or 3 mi away from the site) [1]. Medieval, Roman, Iron Age, Early Bronze Age, and Copper Age periods have all been attested at the site [1]. The Copper Age tell is associated with the Karanovo culture [1]. The tell contains the remains of at least 30 settlements placed one over the other [1]. Various peoples had settled at the tell altogether for more than 6,000 years, at least from the Early Chalcolithic (5000 BCE) onwards [1]. Tell Yunatsite is one of the most important sites for revealing the cultural development of the Early Bronze Age in Thrace [1].

row.name: Bodowyr Burial Chamber
row.description: Bodowyr Burial Chamber is a Neolithic burial chamber made of a few large stacked stones in a farmer's field on the north Wales island of Anglesey [1]. It is located at Bodowyr Farm, 1.25 mi east of Llangaffo [1]. Writing in the Mona Antiqua Restaurata in the early eighteenth century, the antiquarian Henry Rowland described this as "a pretty cromlech standing at the top of a hillock at Bodowyr" [1]. He also mentioned a "small cirque" nearby and the remnants of a cairn from which the stones had mostly been removed for use as building stone; no trace remains of these structures [1]. In 1833 the capstone was said to be supported by four upright stones so one of these would appear to have fallen since then [1]. Bodowyr Burial Chamber is the central burial chamber of a passage grave of a type more frequently found in Ireland [1]. The chamber has three upright stones about a metre high supporting a robust, wedge-shaped capstone [1].

row.name: Fir Clump Stone Circle
row.description: Fir Clump Stone Circle was a stone circle in Burderop Wood near Wroughton, Wiltshire, in South West England [1]. The ring was part of a tradition of stone circle construction that spread throughout much of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany during the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age, over a period between 3300 and 900 BCE [1]. A double concentric circle consisting of sarsen megaliths, the Fir Clump stone circle was oval-shaped [1]. The outer ring measured 107 metres by 86.5 metres in diameter, and the inner ring 86.5 metres by 73.7 metres [1]. It was one of at least seven stone circles that are known to have been erected in the area south of Swindon in northern Wiltshire [1]. Around the 1860s, the megaliths of Fir Clump stone circle were levelled [1]. Some of the fallen megaliths were rediscovered in 1965 by the archaeologist Richard Reiss, who described and measured the monument [1]. In 1969, these stones were removed during construction of the M4 motorway [1].

row.name: Al-Mnaykhrat
row.description: Al-Mnaykhrat or Mnechret is a late sixth-century BC Greek rock-tomb near Marj, in northeastern Libya [1]. The tomb is cut into a cliff on the west side of the Wadi Taybsillu, southeast of the city of Marj [1]. It is clearly visible across the surrounding plain and must have been built for a high-ranking individual, but there is no evidence regarding their identity [1]. The structure is dated to the late sixth century BC on stylistic grounds [1]. The tomb is about 2.15 metres above the ground level [1].

row.name: Swarn Bhandar
row.description: Son Bhandar (Swarn Bhandar) Caves are two Jain man-made caves carved into the base of the Vaibhar Hills in Rajgir, Bihar [1]. Generally dated to the 3rd-4th century AD based on a dedicatory inscription in Gupta script mentioning Jain sage Vairadeva, though some scholars suggest Maurya Empire origins as early as 319 BC [1]. The main cave has a rectangular interior with trapezoidal entrance reminiscent of the earlier Barabar Caves [1]. The name means 'store of gold,' reflecting a persistent legend of hidden treasure within the cave walls [2] [3].

row.name: Al-Dafi Site
row.description: Al-Dafi is a residential archaeological site near Jubail, Saudi Arabia, measuring 235 x 200 meters [1]. It flourished during the era of the intermediate Arab kingdoms [1] [2]. Excavations revealed 149 bags of pottery fragments, Hellenistic architecture with domes, cylindrical vaults, and pillars [1]. The site has links to nearby Thaj, Failaka Island in Kuwait, and Al-Faw in Wadi Al-Dawasir [1].

row.name: Kinniside Stone Circle
row.description: Kinniside Stone Circle is a reconstructed stone circle in the civil parish of Ennerdale and Kinniside in Cumbria [1]. Kinniside Stone Circle is situated next to the fell road from Ennerdale Bridge to Calder Bridge in Cumbria [1]. It consists of 11 small stones of local granite with a possible cairn at its centre [1]. The circle was apparently dismantled in the 18th century by a farmer who used the stones for gate-posts [1]. In 1925 a Doctor Quine of Frizington "restored" the stone circle, setting the stones in concrete [1]. Whether or not he erected the stones in their original stone holes is unclear, and it is unlikely that all of the re-erected stones come from the original circle [1].

row.name: Hatfield Neolithic Trackway
row.description: The Hatfield Neolithic Trackway (Lindholme Trackway) was discovered in 2004, and is one of the oldest known ancient timber trackways in England [1]. The trackway is the second confirmed archaeological structure from Hatfield and Thorne Moors [1]. The Lindholme Trackway dates to around 2900–2500 BC [1]. In October 2004 a number of worked wooden poles were discovered by a local man who was walking across the site [1]. The site was constructed during a period of environmental transformation, where evidence from the coleopteran analyses demonstrated the site was built at a time of increasingly wet and acidic conditions [1]. In 2017 the trackway was designated as a Scheduled Ancient Monument by Historic England [1].

row.name: Ingatambo
row.description: A Formative Period ceremonial center on a natural plateau at 1,066 m elevation in the Huancabamba Valley, Jaen Province, Cajamarca Region, Peru [1] [2]. Excavations led by Atsushi Yamamoto since 2006 identified the Pomahuaca Phase (1200-800 BC) and the Ingatambo Phase (800-550 BC), with evidence of increasingly complex architecture and restricted-access enclosures [1] [2]. The site functioned as a gateway community facilitating interregional exchange, with cultural ties to highland centers like Pacopampa and Kuntur Wasi [2] [3]. Later occupations show Chimu and Inca presence [1] [2].

row.name: Porth Hellick Down
row.description: Porth Hellick Down is a Neolithic and Bronze Age archeological site located on the island of St Mary's, in the Isles of Scilly in Great Britain [1]. The ancient burial monument encompasses a large cairn cemetery that includes at least six entrance graves, other unchambered cairns, and a prehistoric field system [1]. The largest and best preserved entrance grave on the ancient site is a Bronze Age grave (2000-1500 BC) located on the northwestern slope of Porth Hellick Down [1]. The burial monument is situated close to the boundary of a prehistoric field system [1]. The site was excavated by the antiquarian, George Bonsor in 1899 [1]. He named the entrance grave, "The Great Tomb" [1]. Earlier unrecorded excavations at the site had left the burial chamber empty, except for a piece of pumice and a few remnants of late Bronze Age pottery fragments [1].

row.name: Pyrri
row.description: Pyrri was an ancient Roman settlement in the Roman province of Pannonia, situated along a road connecting Poetovio (modern Ptuj, Slovenia) in the north to Siscia (modern Sisak, Croatia) in the south [1] [2] [3] [4]. Archaeological evidence and scholarly research suggest the settlement's location corresponds to the present-day village of Komin in the Sveti Ivan Zelina area of Zagreb County, Croatia [1] [5].

row.name: Troldborg Ring
row.description: The Troldborg Ring is an Iron Age fortification in Vejle Municipality in Denmark, 13 km west of the city of Vejle [1]. It is located at a natural spring on a high point overlooking the Vejle River Valley [1]. The surrounding area is a steep ravine known as the Devil's Valley [1]. The site consists of a raised area of about 1,700 m2 surrounded by a circular rampart [1]. One side is protected by a steep drop of 70 m to the valley floor, while the other side features a 0.5-metre-deep, 2.5-metre-wide moat [1]. The Troldborg Ring was built around the years 100-200 during a period of turbulence in Denmark, and it was used until around the year 400 [1]. It likely served as a refuge during times of violence rather than a permanent dwelling [1]. A considerable amount of ash from massive fires has been found at the site, although the source and timing of these fires is unclear [1].

row.name: Seven Barrows
row.description: Seven Barrows is a Bronze Age barrow cemetery located at Upper Lambourn in the civil parish of Lambourn, Berkshire, England [1] [2]. The site is designated as a biological Site of Special Scientific Interest due to its unimproved chalk grassland supporting over 100 herb species and a rich insect fauna [1] [3]. It is managed by the Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust and is a Scheduled Monument preserving this important prehistoric burial site [1] [3].

row.name: Anta das Pedras Grandes
row.description: The Anta das Pedras Grandes (Dolmen of large stones) is a Late Neolithic (between 4500 and 2000 BC) site located in Ramada e Canecas, in the Odivelas municipality, in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. Excavations in the surrounding area also identified many flint chippings, suggesting that the area was used for the production of flint items [1]. The site was first identified in 1880 by the Portuguese archaeologist Carlos Ribeiro [1]. It is the only surviving dolmen in the immediate area although several were discovered in the late 19th and early 20th centuries [1]. Nevertheless it has suffered considerably from the use of stones by farmers and for construction [1].

row.name: Rockbourne Roman Villa
row.description: Rockbourne Roman villa is located at West Park, near the village of Rockbourne in Hampshire [1]. The villa was discovered in 1942 by a farmer digging out a ferret [1]. Originally the site was occupied by a timber roundhouse with a chalk floor, of a type common in the Late Iron Age [1]. In the 1st century this was replaced by a small rectangular stone house [1]. In 1967 a hoard of 7717 bronze coins was found buried in a pottery jar on the site [1]. By the 4th century the villa was now a large courtyard villa enclosed on at least three sides [1]. In total there were probably around 40 rooms in use [1]. Of particular interest are two much-damaged Roman milestones found re-used in the building fabric of the villa [1].

row.name: Judeir-jo-daro
row.description: Judeir-jo-daro, also known as Damb Judeir, is an archaeological site dating back to the Harappan period in Balochistan, Pakistan [1]. The city, during its time, was a moderate sized settlement with a population of around 20,240 and an area of 2,700,000 square feet (62 acres) [1]. The present day site is a federally protected archaeological site located between Jhatpat and Dera Murad Jamali in the Nasirabad District of Balochistan [1].

row.name: Longovicium
row.description: Longovicium was an auxiliary fort located on Roman Dere Street, in the Roman province of Britannia Inferior [1]. It is located just southwest of Lanchester in the English county of Durham [1]. The fort was situated between Vindomora (Ebchester), and Vinovia (Binchester) on Dere Street, the main Roman road linking Eboracum (York) with Hadrian's Wall [1]. It is about 20 miles south of the wall, and was built on high ground with clear views around the site [1]. A construction slab identifies the Legio XX Valeria Victrix as having built the fort, but this gives no real clue as to when the fort was built [1]. Longovicium is also interesting in having had a copious water supply from two aqueducts, one of which was fed from an impounded source to the west [1]. The dam harnessed the water of 21 springs and was 20 feet high and 110 yards in length, being stone faced and clay lined on the inside [1]. Despite not being on the scale of those supplying cities, the Longovicium aqueduct was nevertheless a significant feat of engineering, being considered one of the best preserved aqueducts in Britain [1].

row.name: Threestoneburn Stone Circle
row.description: Threestoneburn Stone Circle is an archaeological site, a stone circle near the village of Ilderton and about 5 miles south of Wooler, in Northumberland, England [1]. The circle, of the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age, is situated in a large clearing in the modern afforestation of Threestoneburn Wood, formerly overlooking a spacious valley to the east [1]. It is on a slight promontory near the confluence of Threestone Burn and one of its tributaries [1]. Its dimensions are 36 metres north-west to south-east by 30 metres north-east to south-west [1]. There are 16 stones of local pink granite, set about 5.5 metres apart; a larger gap on the east side is thought to be an original entrance [1]. Four of these are upright, with heights 0.7 to 1.3 metres; the rest are recumbent [1]. A thick layer of peat was found above the ground surface [1]. A flint tool was found, and spreads of charcoal which may be the traces of fire-rituals [1].

row.name: Brisworthy Stone Circle
row.description: Brisworthy stone circle is a stone circle on Dartmoor, Devon [1]. It is located three miles east of the A386, northeast of the village of Shaugh Prior [1]. It is three hundred metres from Ringmoor stone row and cairn circle, and is one of the archaeological sites found in the Upper Plym Valley [1]. The stone circle is a slight oval shape with a diameter of around 24 metres [1]. It consists of 24 upright stones which are probably only half the original number [1]. The stones are broad rather than tall, and are less than 1 metre tall [1]. Prior to 1909 most of the stones had fallen [1]. It was restored in that year, and a trial excavation is said to have yielded a small amount of charcoal and one rough flint flake [1].

row.name: Abrigo de la Quebrada
row.description: The Abrigo de la Quebrada is an archaeological site in the municipality of Chelva, in the Spanish Province of Valencia, ca. 65 km northwest of the city of Valencia [1]. It shows evidence of frequent occupation by Neanderthals [1]. The site is on the left bank of a small ravine, the Barranco de Ahillas; it is a rock shelter between 2 and 9 meters deep, and 38 meters long, facing the northwest [1]. Because of the lack of direct sunshine and its exposure, the site was occupied only from June to October, according to Phytoliths and other evidence, including the reuse and resharpening of stone tools [1]. The deposit is around 3 meters thick, and is divided into eight units by archaeologists [1]. Flint tools found at the site give evidence of extensive traffic of Neanderthal populations in the area [1]. While much of the flint was procured locally, some of it came from over 100 kilometers away; knapping was done also by way of the Levallois technique [1].

row.name: Viracochapampa
row.description: Viracochapampa, Huiracochapampa, or Wiracochapampa (possibly from Quechua wiraqucha: mister, sir, gentleman, god; or Wiracocha: one of the greatest Andean divinities; and pampa: plain) is an archaeological site with the remains of a building complex of ancient Peru of pre-Inca times [1]. It was one of the administrative centers of the Wari culture [1]. Viracochapampa is located about 3.5 km north of Huamachuco in the region of La Libertad at an elevation of 3,070 metres [1]. The site was occupied from the late Middle Horizon 1B time to the first decades of period 2A, according to the chronology established by Dorothy Menzel [1]. These correspond to the 7th and 8th centuries of our era [1].

row.name: Griffin Warrior Tomb
row.description: The Griffin Warrior Tomb is a Bronze Age shaft tomb dating to around 1450 BC, near the ancient city of Pylos in Greece [1]. The grave was discovered by a research team sponsored by the University of Cincinnati and led by husband-and-wife archaeologists Jack L. Davis and Sharon Stocker [1]. The tomb site was excavated from May to October 2015 [1]. During the initial six month excavation, the research team uncovered an intact adult male skeleton and excavated 1400 objects including weapons, jewels, armour and silver and gold artifacts [1]. Since 2015, the number of artifacts recovered from the grave has reached over 3500 items, including a historically significant Minoan sealstone called the Pylos Combat Agate and four signet gold rings with detailed images from Minoan mythology [1]. The gravesite was discovered in an olive grove near the ancient Palace of Nestor, within the Bronze Age city of Pylos, in southwest Greece [1].

row.name: Gavur Kalesi
row.description: A Hittite Empire-period rock relief monument in central Anatolia, Turkey, carved on a cliff face atop a natural hill [1] [2]. The relief depicts three deities: two large male figures wearing pointed horned hats (a sign of divinity) and shoes with curled-up toes, carrying swords in their belts, walking toward a less visible seated goddess [1] [2]. First excavated by Von der Osten and Schmidt in 1930, with major surveys by Stephen Lumsden (1993-1998) for Bilkent University [2].

row.name: Piercebridge Roman Bridge
row.description: Piercebridge Roman Bridge is the ruin of a Roman bridge over the River Tees [1]. The bridge carried the Roman road Dere Street across the river [1]. Piercebridge Roman Fort guarded the bridge [1]. The first bridge was built around 90 AD, but this may have been replaced by a second bridge after it was washed away [1]. What remains of the bridge are massive masonry blocks that formed at least five piers [1]. The remains were discovered in 1972 during gravel quarrying [1]. The stone blocks are up to 1.5 metres long and the total bridge structure was 123 metres long [1].

row.name: Box Gully Archaeological Site
row.description: Box Gully is an Aboriginal archaeological site on the shore of saline Lake Tyrrell in the Mallee region of northern Victoria, Australia [1]. The site contains remains of a small hunting camp that produced radiocarbon dates of 26,600-32,000 years BP, making it one of the earliest known occupied sites in the region [1].

row.name: Veluška Tumba
row.description: Veluška Tumba is an ancient settlement from Neolithic times, near the village of Porodin in the Republic of Macedonia, close to Bitola [1]. The site is an artificially raised mound shaped like a truncated cone, with an elliptical base laid out east to west [2]. The mound measures 250 m in length, 150 m in width and 0.70 to 5 m in height [2]. The excavations found a cultural layer four metres thick, filled with habitation remains spread over four horizons [2].

row.name: Poor Lot Barrow Cemetery
row.description: Poor Lot Barrow Cemetery is an archaeological site, a group of Bronze Age round barrows, near the A35 road about 2 miles west of Winterbourne Abbas, in Dorset, England [1]. Although the barrows are situated not on a ridge or hilltop, as is usually found, but on relatively low-lying ground, the site is near the head of a valley descending to the east [1]. Most are south of the A35 road, with a few north of the road [1]. They date from about 1500 BC [1]. The barrows, individually or in groups, are separately listed as ancient monuments [1]. There is a minor plateau on the west of the site, from which all the barrows can be seen [1].

row.name: Pughjaredda
row.description: Pughjaredda (also spelled Poghjaredda) is a megalithic archaeological site in the commune of Sotta, southern Corsica, dating to the Middle Neolithic period (ca. 5000-4000 BC) [1] [2] [3] [4]. The site features dolmens, menhirs, and stone circles, along with evidence of domestic dwelling and funerary activities [2]. Studies at Pughjaredda have provided key insights into Corsican-Sardinian megalithism [2].

row.name: Blackbury Camp
row.description: An Iron Age hillfort near Southleigh in Devon [1] [2]. The oval enclosure measures roughly 200 m by 100 m, defended by a rampart about 3 m high and 10 m wide with an outer ditch up to 12 m across [2]. Its single south entrance was protected by timber gates, possibly within a gate-tower [2]. Excavations uncovered a hut, cooking pit, oven, over 1,000 slingstones, Iron Age pottery, iron slag, whetstones, and spindle whorls [2] [3] [4]. Managed by English Heritage, it is interpreted as a defended homestead of a wealthy Iron Age family [2] [3].

row.name: Atella
row.description: Atella was an ancient Oscan city of Campania, located 20km directly north of Naples [1]. The ruins of the city walls, private houses, the so-called garden of Virgil and many tombs remain, on sites in the comuni of Frattaminore, Orta di Atella, Sant'Arpino and Succivo [1]. Atella was a city of Oscan origin, one of the oldest in Campania and one of the first to have obtained the Roman civitas [1]. It was crossed by the Via Atellana, which led southwest to Cumae and northeast to Capua [1]. Atella is not mentioned until the Second Punic War, when, although an independent city striking its own coinage, it was allied with Capua and the other Campanian cities in siding with Carthage after the battle of Cannae [1]. It was occupied by Rome in 210 BC, the chief citizens executed and the survivors enslaved or exiled to Calatia; the city was refounded as a home for the refugees from Nuceria [1]. In the 1st century BC, Cicero speaks highly of it and appears to have been its patron; it continued into imperial times as a municipium [1].

row.name: Nichoria
row.description: Nichoria is a site in Messenia, on a ridgetop near modern Rizomylos, at the northwestern corner of the Messenian Gulf [1]. During the Helladic period it was part of the Mycenaean civilisation [1]. Nichoria became subordinate to Pylos and lost the use of its megaron [1]. Nichoria was a major outpost of Pylos's "Trans-Aigolaia" province [1]. Nichoria was destroyed in the same event which claimed the main palace at Pylos [1]. The University of Minnesota Messenia Expedition under William Andrew McDonald surveyed the area in the 1960s, and began excavating Nichoria in 1969 [1]. On the foot of the Nichoria acropolis there was discovered a burial circle, comprising a collective burial of 7 people; it was in use until the LH IIIA period, when the adjacent large tholos tomb was built [1].

row.name: Notgrove Long Barrow
row.description: Notgrove Long Barrow is a prehistoric long barrow burial mound in Gloucestershire, England [1]. It consists of a large mound with a passage running through the centre and several small chambers opening off it [1]. Human remains were interred in these chambers [1]. It is unlikely that any of these remains are still within the mound, as the barrow was open for thousands of years before being sealed in 1976 to prevent further damage to the site [1]. The barrow was surveyed in 1974 and the dimensions were estimated at 46 metres long, 30 metres wide and 1.7 metres high [1].

row.name: Massinissa Mausoleum
row.description: The Soumaâ du Khroub, also called the royal Numidian mausoleum of El Khroub and nicknamed the Tomb of Massinissa, is a Numidian funerary monument at El Khroub in the wilaya of Constantine, Algeria [1]. The square-plan tower mausoleum rises 30 metres, and analysis of the objects found in it dates the monument to the second half of the 2nd century BC [1]. A document of the Cirta National Museum records excavations by French archaeologists between 1915 and 1916 that make a mixed Greco-Punic style of the stones likely [1]. The tomb held two superimposed compartments separated by slabs and contained three intact funerary urns, as well as fragments of a sword, a helmet, a tunic, a coat of mail and bones [1]. The finds from the tomb are exhibited in the Cirta National Museum [1]. Since 2002 the monument has stood on the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list under the Royal Mausoleums of Numidia and Mauretania [1].

row.name: Pons Aelius
row.description: Pons Aelius, or Newcastle Roman Fort, was an auxiliary castra and small Roman settlement on Hadrian's Wall in the Roman province of Britannia Inferior, situated on the north bank of the River Tyne close to the centre of present-day Newcastle upon Tyne [1]. Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle [1]. The Latin name means Aelian Bridge and can be traced back to when emperor Hadrian visited Britain in 122 and first saw the need for a frontier wall [1]. The fort is thought to have been 1.53 acres, small by Roman standards [1]. Much of the fort remains buried underneath the medieval Castle Keep, which gave the city of Newcastle its name [1]. Excavations around the castle keep and dredging of the Tyne yielded finds typical of Roman encampments [1]. A dedication to emperor Hadrian's mother, Domitia Paulina Major, attests the presence of the Cohors Ulpia Traiana Cugernorum civium Romanorum as evidently being stationed at Pons Aelius at the beginning of the third century [1].

row.name: Karta
row.description: Karta is the Kaurna name Karta Pintingga, meaning Island of the Dead, for the island known as Kangaroo Island in the state of South Australia [1]. Kangaroo Island was separated from mainland Australia around 10,000 years ago, when sea level rose after the last glacial period [1]. Stone tools and shell middens on the island show that Aboriginal people once lived on Kangaroo Island [1]. The island's native population, sometimes called the Kartan people, disappeared from the archaeological record after the land became an island around 10,000 years ago [1]. The Kartan industry produced a large quantity of exceptionally large stone tools, probably more than 10,000 years ago, that were found on Karta [2].

row.name: Capela de São Dinis
row.description: The Anta de Pavia is a Neolithic dolmen erected between the 4th and 3rd millennia BC, composed of seven enormous orthostats topped by a massive capstone [1] [2]. The chamber was converted into a Christian chapel dedicated to Sao Dinis, with a bell tower, cross, and an altar decorated with 18th-century Lisbon azulejo tiles added to the interior [1] [3]. Classified as a Portuguese National Monument since 1910, it stands in the centre of Pavia village in the Alentejo region [1] [4].

row.name: Roman Villa of Santo André de Almoçageme
row.description: A Roman villa in Colares, Sintra, occupied from the 1st century AD until at least the mid-5th century [1] [2]. An early 20th-century road cut through the central peristyle, dividing the site into the pars urbana (manor house) to the north and pars rustica (agricultural annexes) to the south [1]. The manor house contained the largest group of mosaics identified in the Lisbon region [1]. Finds are housed at the Archaeological Museum of Sao Miguel de Odrinhas [3] [4].

row.name: Wor Barrow
row.description: Wor Barrow is a Neolithic long barrow on Cranborne Chase, near Sixpenny Handley in Dorset [1]. Excavated by Augustus Pitt Rivers in 1893-94, it was the first Neolithic long barrow completely excavated and recorded to modern standards [1] [2]. Radiocarbon dating places the primary burials in the 37th century BC [2] [3]. Six adult males under 45 were found within a timber mortuary enclosure [1] [2]. The barrow had two construction phases: first a rectangular ditched mortuary enclosure, then a chalk mound covering the entire structure [1] [2].

row.name: Tarmatambo
row.description: Tarmatambo or Tarmatampu (possibly from Tarma an ethnic group, Quechua tampu inn) is an archaeological site in the Junín Region in Peru [1]. It is located in the Tarma Province, Tarma District, in the community of the same name [1]. The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage by Resolución Directoral Nacional No. 040/INC on January 29, 2002 [1].

row.name: Aves Ditch
row.description: Aves Ditch is an Iron Age ditch and bank structure running about 3 miles on a northeast to southwest alignment in the Cherwell District of Oxfordshire [1]. It was once believed to have been a Roman road but excavation has shown it to be a boundary dyke of Iron Age date that was reused in the Anglo-Saxon period [1]. A skull found in the ditch was dated to the Anglo-Saxon period [1]. Both Sauer and Lambrick have suggested that the Aves Ditch along with the North Oxfordshire Grim’s Ditch and the South Oxfordshire Grim’s Ditch may have formed the boundary between the Iron Age tribes of the Dobunni and the Catuvellauni [1].

row.name: Sohr Damb
row.description: Sohr Damb, c. 3800–2300 BC, is an archaeological site near Nal in central Balochistan, Pakistan that begins before the Indus Valley Civilization featuring Togau, Kili Ghul Mohammad, and Kechi Beg pottery styles [1]. It has also been known as Naal, Balochistan, and gave its name to the prehistoric Amri-Nal culture, which is attributed to the dual typesites of Amri and Nal [1]. The site extends around 4,5 hectares; the mound (mostly geologically formed) is 13 m high [1]. The excavations reveal four periods of occupation, and they could be further divided into several sub-periods [1]. The locality was first discovered in 1903 [1]. Since 2001, the site has been systematically excavated by the German Archaeological Institute and the Department of Archeology and Museums, Government of Pakistan [1]. Domesticated cattle bones are plentiful in the settlement, and bull figurines are also found [1].

row.name: Archaeological Site of Palaepaphos
row.description: Ancient city-kingdom at modern Kouklia, home to the principal Sanctuary of Aphrodite in the Aegean world, where pilgrims worshipped from the 12th century BC until the Roman ban on pagan religion in 391 AD [1] [2]. The goddess was venerated not as a statue but as an aniconic conical stone on an open-air altar [1] [2]. First Cypriot site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980 [1] [3] [4].

row.name: Brocavum
row.description: Brocavum is the Latin name of a Roman fort at Brougham near Penrith, Cumbria [1]. The fort survives as earthworks, but no excavation of these has been carried out so far [1]. With the rivers Eamont and Lowther flowing nearby and meeting to the west, the site had natural defences [1]. Six dedications to the local deity Belatucadrus were discovered at Brougham, suggesting perhaps "that his worship was centred there" [1]. The medieval Brougham Castle now occupies part of the site [1]. It is known that stones from the Roman fort were used in the construction of the castle, as a Roman tombstone can be seen in a passageway in the keep, used as a ceiling slab [1]. The fort is scheduled as an Ancient Monument, along with the castle, as "Brougham Roman fort and Brougham Castle" [1].

row.name: Featherwood Roman Camps
row.description: Featherwood Roman Camps are neighbouring archaeological sites in Northumberland, England, 1 mile north of Featherwood and about 3 miles east of Byrness [1]. The remains of two Roman camps, near Dere Street, are scheduled monuments [1]. The two camps, about 500 metres apart, are situated on either side of Dere Street, a Roman road in use between AD 78 and AD 211 running from Eboracum into Scotland [1]. The camps date from the 1st century AD [1]. They are thought to have been used by soldiers advancing northwards, and by smaller groups employed in routine maintenance [1]. Chew Green and Bremenium, nearby Roman encampments on Dere Street, lie to the north and south [1].

row.name: La Joyanca
row.description: La Joyanca is the modern name for a pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site located south of the San Pedro Martir river in the Petén department of Guatemala [1]. The site was discovered in 1994 during the construction of the Xan-La Libertad oil pipeline in Guatemala [1]. It was immediately recognized as an important, undiscovered Classic period (AD 200-900) Maya city and became the focus of an archaeological project [1]. La Joyanca was occupied for well over 1000 years [1]. Dates from the site range from the Late Preclassic (200 BC) to the Terminal Classic/Postclassic (AD 1000) [1]. Population levels reached their height here during the Late Classic (AD 600-900); during this era the rulers of La Joyanca embarked upon an ambitious building project in two areas, dubbed the Plaza Principal and the Grupo Guacamaya [1]. The Grupo Guacamaya, a complex of vaulted rooms and corridors, may have served as their palace and thus the seat of local government [1]. The Grupo Guacamaya was briefly occupied by squatters in the 10th century, but the area was ultimately abandoned by AD 1000 [1].

row.name: Blue Man-i'-th'-Moss
row.description: Blue Man-i'-th'-Moss is a 2-metre-tall standing stone on Wheeldale Moor in the North York Moors, along the route of the Lyke Wake Walk [1]. Though now used as a parish boundary marker, it is believed to date from pre-Roman times [1]. The stone is heavily weathered and bears an engraved 'E 1841' date on its south face [1].

row.name: Longstone of Minchinhampton
row.description: The Longstone of Minchinhampton is a standing stone on Minchinhampton Common, Minchinhampton in Gloucestershire, England [1]. The Longstone is a large piece of oolitic limestone standing upright in a field, known as Longstone Field, 1 mile east of the Minchinhampton village [1]. It is 7.5 feet high and 6 feet wide, with natural holes through its 15 inches width [1]. Nearby, 12 yards to the south west, there is a fallen standing stone which has been built into a dry stone wall, and may have once formed a stone pair with the Longstone [1]. The area has numerous barrows and near the Longstone ornaments, flint and arrowheads have all been found [1]. The stone was believed to be able to cure infants of maladies such as measles and whooping cough, by passing the child through one of the natural holes [1].

row.name: Gamelands Stone Circle
row.description: Gamelands stone circle (or Orton stone circle) is a stone circle at the foot of Knott Hill in Cumbria, England [1]. Gamelands stone circle lies between the village of Orton and the hamlet of Raisbeck [1]. It is an oval enclosure of around 40 large stones together with three smaller stones [1]. The stones are set into a slight bank [1]. The stones are all below one metre in height and are arranged in an oval of 42 metres by 35 metres [1]. Around 1862 some of the stones were buried or blasted [1]. Ploughing uncovered two worked flints and a probable cist-slab [1].

row.name: Ebsbury
row.description: The site of Ebsbury, in Wiltshire, England, includes the remains of an Iron Age enclosed settlement, field system and possible hill fort, and a Romano-British enclosed settlement [1]. The site occupies the spur of a downland hill with the possible hill fort enclosure measuring approximately 700 m by 400 m, inside of which lie the remains of a field system with two further smaller oval enclosures and one triangular enclosure [1]. To the north and east sides of the site the contours of the hill have been reinforced by several banks [1]. The site of an Iron Age settlement lies to the eastern end of the site [1]. The site was subject to archaeological surveys and excavations in 1906 by S.W. Doughty [1]. Finds include a Neolithic perforated mace-head and two Roman coin hoards [1]. The latter were found buried in two earthenware pots; the coins date from between AD 337 and AD 408, and were found with the remains of a glass vessel, and six silver rings [1].

row.name: Jinkiori
row.description: Jinkiori is a petroglyph site in Paucartambo Province, Cusco, Peru, centered on a large monolith near the Queros River, about two hours' walk from Pilcopata [1]. The engravings on the Monolith of Jinkiori have Amazonian origins and include abstract representations possibly linked to cosmological beliefs and ayahuasca use [1]. The carvings may have been created by ancestors of the Huachipaeri, an indigenous group still living in the Kosñipata valley [1]. Features include a small basin possibly used for preparing chicha and a distinctive key-shaped engraving [1].

row.name: Tanqa Tanqa
row.description: Tanqa Tanqa is a major archaeological pukara (fortified hilltop settlement) of the Lupaca culture, located at an elevation of 3,974 m [1]. Dating to the Late Intermediate Period (AD 1000-1450), it emerged after the collapse of the Tiwanaku civilization [1]. The site covers roughly 30 hectares and features circular domestic structures, chullpas (funerary towers), and agricultural terraces [1] [2]. It was declared part of Peru's National Cultural Heritage on 17 July 2001 [3] [4].

row.name: Hell Stone
row.description: The Hell Stone is a badly-restored Neolithic dolmen on Portesham Hill in Dorset, England [1]. It is just to the north of the village of Portesham, and approximately three-quarters of a mile southeast of the Valley of Stones [1]. The Hell Stone is situated at the head of a dry valley system in the parish of Portesham [1]. The burial chamber is at the southeast end of a rectangular mound [1]. The mound is 24 metres long and orientated northwest to southeast [1]. The mound tapers from 12 to 8 metres in width from the southeast end to the northwest end, and it is 1 metre high [1]. The chamber was badly restored in 1866 when eight men re-erected the stones, arranging them radially "rather like the slices of a cake" and supporting a large capstone [1].

row.name: Stonehenge Cursus
row.description: The Stonehenge Cursus is a large Neolithic cursus monument on Salisbury plain, near to Stonehenge in Wiltshire, England [1]. Radiocarbon dating of a red deer antler pick discovered at the bottom of the western terminal ditch suggests that the Stonehenge Cursus was first constructed between 3630 and 3375 BCE [1]. It is just under 3 km long, and is roughly 100 m wide [1]. Because of a slight difference in the alignment of its north and south ditches, it widens to a point nearly 150 m near its western end [1]. It is roughly aligned east–west and is oriented toward the sunrise on the spring and autumn equinoxes [1]. There is a Bronze Age round barrow inside the western end of the enclosure, and a large Neolithic long barrow was constructed at its east terminal [1]. William Stukeley was the first antiquarian to identify and record the Stonehenge Cursus, although he incorrectly assumed it to be Roman in origin [1].

row.name: Devil's Arrows
row.description: The Devil's Arrows are three aligned standing stones located outside Boroughbridge in North Yorkshire, England, near to where the A168 road crosses the River Ure [1]. The outer stones are 360 and 200 feet away from the central stone and form an almost straight line, running NNW–SSE [1]. Erected during the Stone Age and distinctively grooved by millennia of rainfall, the tallest stone is 22.5 feet in height, making this the second tallest menhir in the United Kingdom after the 25 feet tall Rudston Monolith in the East Riding of Yorkshire [1]. In 2026, scientists at Curtin University and the University of York used isotopic fingerprinting to show that the stones originated at Brimham Rocks, about 11 miles to the west [1]. The study also found that the Battle Cross at Aldborough has the same geological fingerprint as the surviving Arrows, supporting its identification as a repurposed fourth stone from the original monument [1]. The stones are part of a prehistoric complex concentrated around the River Ure [1]. The name is mentioned by the antiquary John Aubrey, who visited and drew the stones in 1687 [1].

row.name: Ballylumford Dolmen
row.description: Portal tomb on the Islandmagee peninsula, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, situated in a private front garden near Ballylumford power station [1] [2]. Known locally as the Druid's Altar, it consists of four upright stones supporting a heavy capstone, with a fallen stone inside that may have blocked the tomb entrance [1] [3]. A wall plaque dates it to approximately 2000-1600 BC, though it could be the remains of an even earlier passage grave [1]. It is a State Care Historic Monument in the townland of Ballylumford [1].

row.name: Maray Qalla
row.description: Maray Qalla (Quechua maran, maray batan or grindstone, maray to tear down, to knock down, qalla carved stone, cobblestone; circular spindle disk; cheek, also spelled Maraycalla, Maraycalle) is an archaeological site in Peru [1]. It is situated in the Ancash Region, Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald Province [1]. Maray Qalla lies at a section of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system [1].

row.name: Eggardon Hill
row.description: Eggardon Hill is a prehistoric hillfort on a hill in Dorset [1]. It is located on chalk uplands approximately four miles to the east of the town of Bridport [1]. The earliest archaeological features on the hill are linear earthworks which cross the interior [1]. These were partially excavated during 1963-6 and found to be Bronze Age [1]. There are also two bowl barrows within the area of the hillfort that were dated to the Middle Bronze Age [1]. The large multivallate hillfort dates from the Iron Age [1]. The surviving earthworks enclose an area of approximately 21ha in total [1].

row.name: Lower Swat Valley
row.description: Barikot is identified as ancient Bazira and has been excavated by an Italian mission since 1984 [1] [2]. The region preserves remains of the Gandhara grave culture and buildings of the Shahi Period [2] [3]. Chinese pilgrim Hsuan-Tsang reported 1,400 monasteries in Swat during his 7th-century visit [4].

row.name: Teteles de Santo Nombre
row.description: Teteles de Santo Nombre is an ancient town in Puebla, Mexico, occupied for over a millennium [1] [2]. The site features two restored pyramidal structures standing 7 and 14 metres tall, exhibiting architectural similarities to the Teotihuacan civilization [2]. These pyramids, named Piramide de los Caracoles (Shells Pyramid) and Piramide de los Cascabeles (Rattles Pyramid), were restored and consolidated as part of archaeological work at the site [2].

row.name: Tŷ Newydd Burial Chamber
row.description: Tŷ Newydd Burial Chamber is a Neolithic dolmen located northeast of the village of Llanfaelog on the Isle of Anglesey in Wales [1]. Tŷ Newydd burial chamber is a ruined megalithic dolmen set up on a natural outcrop and would originally have been covered with a mound or cairn [1]. The capstone measures 4.0 metres by 1.8 metres and is up to 1.2 metres thick [1]. The capstone is cracked and rests on three of the four remaining uprights [1]. The chamber was excavated in August 1935 by Charles Phillips [1]. The chamber was found to be about 2.8 metres by 1.2 metres, and its area was defined by a spread of charcoal with a hearth at the eastern end, where there was thought to have been a second chamber or passage [1]. The finds included five flint flakes, a burnt flint arrowhead, a small chip from a polished flint axe, and nine small fragments of pottery [1]. Phillips believed that the pottery fragments were from the Beaker culture, and thus might represent Bronze Age reuse of an earlier Neolithic monument [1].

row.name: Temple of Segesta
row.description: The Temple of Segesta is an ancient temple built around 420 BC in the hilltop archaeological area of Calatafimi Segesta in western Sicily [1] [2]. The well-preserved structure features six by fourteen Doric columns and was likely never completed, lacking a roof and interior cella [2] [3]. Located in the province of Trapani, the temple remains one of the best-preserved examples of classical Greek architecture in Sicily [1].

row.name: Prehistoric Rock-Art Site of Pala Pinta
row.description: The Prehistoric Rock-Art Site of Pala Pinta is a rock shelter in Alijó, Portugal, in the parish of Carlão e Amieiro [1] [2]. The paintings cover a granite surface 12 metres long and 2.5 metres high, featuring monochromatic ochre imagery of radial forms, dots, and anthropomorphic figures [1]. Experts date the art to the Chalcolithic period (3rd millennium BC) [3] [4].

row.name: Ara trium Galliarum
row.description: The Ara trium Galliarum ("Altar of the Three Gauls") was a Roman sanctuary at Lugdunum (modern Lyon, France), founded by Drusus at the confluence of the Rhone and Saone rivers [1] [2] [3]. Consecrated to Roma and Augustus, it served as the central meeting place where representatives of the three Gallic provinces -- Aquitania, Belgica, and Lugdunensis -- gathered annually [1] [2]. The altar bore the names of 60 Gallic tribes and featured prominently on coins from the Lugdunum mint [2] [3].

row.name: Brauroneion
row.description: The Brauroneion was the sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia on the Athenian Acropolis, located in the southwest corner of the Acropolis plateau, between the Chalkotheke and the Propylaea in Greece [1]. It was originally dedicated during the reign of Peisistratos [1]. The sanctuary on the Acropolis was of an unusual trapezoidal shape and did not contain a formal temple [1]. Instead, a portico or stoa served that function [1]. The stoa measured circa 38 by 6.8 m; it stood in front of the southern Acropolis wall, facing north [1]. In 346 BC, a second cult statue was erected [1]. According to Pausanias, it was a work by Praxiteles [1]. Pausanias also records the presence of an over-life-sized bronze horse representing the Trojan Horse [1].
