row.old_value: A small Roman town on a road to the River Trent. The settlement grew 600 meters from the nearest fort — a civilian community in the shadow of the military.
row.new_value: The Derby Racecourse Roman settlement was the third settlement in Derby or Derventio which was a small town in the Roman province of Britannia.

row.old_value: A settlement at 4,115 metres with the earliest evidence of reduced mobility in the Lake Titicaca Basin, from 3400-1600 BC. Three pithouses were excavated.
1st-century AD Roman frontier line stretching 135 km across the Swabian Jura, anchored at Rottweil in the southwest and Heidenheim in the northeast. It marked the outer edge of Rome.
row.new_value: The Alb Limes is a Roman frontier fortification or limes of the late 1st century AD in the Swabian Jura, also known as the Swabian Alb.

row.old_value: The largest stone circle in its county, with eighteen sarsen stones in an egg-shaped oval 27 metres across. It has never been formally excavated.
row.new_value: Kingston Russell is the largest surviving stone circle in Dorset. The ring consists of eighteen stones, the longest of which are located at the north of the circle.

row.old_value: A dolmen called "Stone of the Moors" — a name locals gave to ancient structures they couldn't explain. Neolithic people built it around 4000-2500 BC.
row.new_value: The Anta da Pedra dos Mouros was reportedly first identified in 1856 by Carlos Ribeiro but he did not have a chance to carry out excavations until 1876 after receiving approval from the landowner.

row.old_value: Early Saka kurgans from the 8th–6th century BC in a river basin. Carbon-14 dating pushed the timeline of Saka culture earlier than expected.
At 3,600 meters on Mount Tawqaray, about 5 km southeast of Cusco, Wayna Tawqaray commands the Watanay River valley. Its position above key routes marks it as a high-altitude Inca landscape node.
row.new_value: Wayna Tawqaray is situated at a height of about 3,600 metres on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray.

row.old_value: A small cave intermittently occupied from 4000 to 2000 BC. Formed by karst erosion, it preserves layers of Neolithic and Chalcolithic habitation in tight stratigraphy.
row.new_value: The first formal archaeological excavation was carried out in 1955 by a team led by Hipólito Cabaço.

row.old_value: A stone circle dismantled by a farmer in the 18th century for gatepost material. In 1925, a local doctor "restored" the 11 stones to approximate positions.
1st-century AD Roman settlement in Pannonia, sited on the road between Poetovio and Siscia. Believed to lie near today's village of Komin — a minor node in Rome's Danubian road network.
Over 40 barrows clustered at Upper Lambourn, Berkshire, the earliest dating to c. 2200 BC. The 4-hectare site is also a biological SSSI — its chalk grassland supports more than 100 herb species.
A Roman courtyard villa from the 1st century AD with well-preserved mosaic floors. It grew from a simple farmhouse into a sprawling estate.
row.new_value: By the 4th century the villa was now a large courtyard villa enclosed on at least three sides.

row.old_value: A rock shelter frequently occupied by Neanderthals who hunted horses, deer, and rabbits here. Stone tools and charred bones fill multiple occupation layers.
row.new_value: Flint tools found at the site give evidence of extensive traffic of Neanderthal populations in the area.

row.old_value: Shaft tomb from 1450 BC near ancient Pylos, unearthed in 2015 with 1,400 intact objects — weapons, jewels, and carved gems beside a warrior skeleton. Among the greatest Bronze Age finds in decades.
row.new_value: The gravesite was discovered in an olive grove near the ancient Palace of Nestor, within the Bronze Age city of Pylos.

row.old_value: A Neolithic settlement from the 5th millennium BC where pottery and stone tools were found. The earliest layers of habitation in this region date to this period.
Forty-four round barrows from around 1500 BC occupy low-lying ground near Winterbourne Abbas — unusual for a barrow cemetery, which typically sits on a ridge. The site lies near the head of a valley.
row.new_value: Poor Lot Barrow Cemetery is an archaeological site, a group of Bronze Age round barrows, near the A35 road about 2 miles west of Winterbourne Abbas, in Dorset.

row.old_value: Hilltop fort on a Devon ridgeline above valleys formed by Coly River tributaries. The terrain provided natural defence on three sides, concentrating fortification on the exposed eastern approach.
3rd-century BC Oscan city 20 km north of Naples, crossed by the Via Atellana. Atella gave its name to the Fabula Atellana — an early form of Roman comic theatre that shaped Latin comedy.
row.new_value: Atella was a city of Oscan origin, one of the oldest in Campania and one of the first to have obtained the Roman civitas.

row.old_value: A central passage and small chambers held human remains for thousands of years before the barrow was sealed in 1976. The mound measures 27 by 18 metres and dates to the 3rd millennium BC.
row.new_value: Notgrove Long Barrow is a prehistoric long barrow burial mound in Gloucestershire.

row.old_value: Guarding the north bank of the Tyne from the 2nd to 4th century AD, Pons Aelius sat on Hadrian's Wall at present-day Newcastle. Its name — Aelius's Bridge — honoured Emperor Hadrian's family name.
row.new_value: Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle.

row.old_value: A 2.3-metre limestone standing stone with natural holes worn through it. Folklore says passing a child through the holes could cure rickets and other ailments.
Declared a National Cultural Heritage. Tanqa Tanqa sits in the Zepita District, Chucuito Province, Puno Region — an archaeological site on the Andean altiplano near the frontier with Bolivia.
Four uprights bear a tilting capstone at the north-west tip of Islandmagee — known locally as the Druid's Altar, dating to around 2000 BC or the stripped remains of an earlier passage grave.
A prehistoric hillfort with triple ramparts enclosing Bronze Age burial mounds inside its walls. The barrows predate the fort by centuries.
A ruined Neolithic dolmen set on a natural rock outcrop, once covered by a mound or cairn. The cracked capstone measures 4 by 1.8 meters and is 1.2 meters thick.
row.new_value: Tŷ Newydd burial chamber is a ruined megalithic dolmen set up on a natural outcrop and would originally have been covered with a mound or cairn.

row.old_value: A 1st-century BC altar where representatives of 60 Gallic tribes gathered annually to pledge loyalty to Rome. It was the political center of Roman-controlled Gaul.
47 upright stones, 30 recumbent, and 4 outliers in an oval 43 by 40 m on Bodmin Moor. Cornish circles use local granite and typically count far more stones than inland examples.
row.new_value: Stannon is an example of Alexander Thom's Type A flattened circle, being noticeably flattened on the north side.

row.old_value: A late Neolithic stone circle with 32 stones and cup-and-ring carvings. These are among the northernmost examples of such rock art found in Britain.
row.new_value: The circle, of the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age, is situated in a large clearing in the modern afforestation of Threestoneburn Wood, formerly overlooking a spacious valley to the east.

row.old_value: A Wari administrative center at over 3,000 meters elevation. The Wari built standardized planned cities across their empire, connected by road networks.
row.new_value: Viracochapampa is located about 3.5 km north of Huamachuco in the region of La Libertad at an elevation of 3,070 metres.

row.old_value: Roman fort at Brougham near Penrith, with early occupation linked to the revolt of Venutius around 70 AD. Artefacts from the excavated cemetery span the 2nd and 3rd centuries.
row.new_value: The fort survives as earthworks, but no excavation of these has been carried out so far. With the rivers Eamont and Lowther flowing nearby and meeting to the west, the site had natural defences.

row.old_value: Badly botched in the 19th century, this 3400 BC Portesham Hill dolmen had its stones haphazardly re-erected. The burial chamber originally sat at the end of a 24-metre mound.
row.new_value: The chamber was badly restored in 1866 when eight men re-erected the stones, arranging them radially "rather like the slices of a cake" and supporting a large capstone.

row.old_value: The Derby Racecourse Roman settlement was the third settlement in Derby or Derventio which was a small town in the Roman province of Britannia.
row.new_value: Beside the Roman road to Sawley on the River Trent, 600m east of the Derventio fort in Little Chester, lies the Derby Racecourse Roman Settlement, founded around AD 90.

row.old_value: A hillfort from around 700 BC was later overbuilt by a Roman-era stone settlement with an attached field system on this Northumberland moorland. Two occupations share the same defensible ground.
row.new_value: On a small hill above the Aln valley, Jenny's Lantern keeps an Iron Age hillfort and the remains of at least 15 stone-founded circular huts. A lacrymatory was found here in 1824.

row.old_value: Two ditches enclosing a circular area 79 metres in diameter near Fowey in Cornwall. Occupied from the 5th or 4th century BC, later linked by medieval romance to the legend of Tristan and Iseult.
row.new_value: Two ditches form the perimeter of Castle Dore, an Iron Age hill fort near Golant. Digging inside it from 1936, Ralegh Radford found postholes of huts from at least two phases of occupation.

row.old_value: Excavations traced roughly 80 individuals buried here between 4000 and 2500 BC — part of a trio of megalithic tombs clustered together in what is now Queluz.
row.new_value: An 8 metre corridor led into the Anta do Monte Abraão, a Neolithic dolmen that excavations suggest was a tomb for about 80 individuals. Its finds include flint arrowheads and stone axes.

row.old_value: Dartmoor megaliths including stone rows, a fourfold stone circle, and standing stones from 3300–500 BC. Four concentric circles in one site is exceptionally rare.
row.new_value: Across a ridge of Dartmoor, Shovel Down holds stone rows of probable Bronze Age date and the Fourfold Circle, four concentric stone circles where a turf-covered cairn keeps a robbed cist.

row.old_value: The fifth fort on Hadrian's Wall, garrisoned by Roman cavalry. Coins, tombstones, sandals, and a spear point have surfaced from beneath the modern village.
row.new_value: The Military Road now cuts through Hunnum, the fifth fort on Hadrian's Wall, built between 122 and 126 AD. A slab from its west gate names the Legio VI Victrix as its first builders.

row.old_value: 24 broad upright stones form a 24-metre oval on Dartmoor -- roughly half the original number. Located 300 metres from Ringmoor Stone Row and Cairn Circle in the Upper Plym Valley.
row.new_value: On Dartmoor, Brisworthy Stone Circle keeps 24 broad, low stones in a slight oval, probably only half the original number. A trial dig is said to have yielded charcoal and one flint flake.

row.old_value: A site in the Cholistan Desert where ceramics dating to 5000 BC were found — evidence of the ancient Hakra civilization that predates the Indus Valley cities.
row.new_value: Once called Pholra, Fort Abbas guarded caravan routes across the Cholistan Desert, where hundreds of ancient settlements line a dry riverbed and the earliest finds are Hakra Ware.

row.old_value: The Alb Limes is a Roman frontier fortification or limes of the late 1st century AD in the Swabian Jura, also known as the Swabian Alb.
row.new_value: Across the Swabian Alb runs the Alb Limes, a Roman frontier of the late 1st century AD, stretching just under 135 kilometres from Rottweil in the southwest to Heidenheim an der Brenz.

row.old_value: A ring of stones at 207 metres on a Dorset downland ridge — either a Bronze Age stone circle or kerbstones from a lost round barrow. Archaeologists still debate which explanation fits the evidence.
row.new_value: The stones of Hampton Down Stone Circle were not in their original position. A May 1965 excavation found the original oval circle a few feet to the west, on a ridge 680 feet above sea level.

row.old_value: Stannon is an example of Alexander Thom's Type A flattened circle, being noticeably flattened on the north side.
row.new_value: On Bodmin Moor near St. Breward, Stannon Stone Circle is a ring of stones noticeably flattened on its north side. Stand at its supposed centre, and Rough Tor marks a point north of east.

row.old_value: Late 4th-century BC Macedonian tomb at ancient Lete, with a monumental facade and two vaulted chambers. Discovered among cist graves on the road between Thessaloniki and Langadas.
row.new_value: Under an earthen tumulus 19.5 m high and 76 m in diameter, the Tomb of Macridy Bey hides two vaulted chambers behind a facade of Ionic columns, already looted when it was excavated in 1910.

row.old_value: A Neolithic cairn from the 4th–3rd millennium BC atop a prominent tor on Bodmin Moor. The rocky outcrop served as a landmark visible for miles.
row.new_value: On Bodmin Moor, Showery Tor's erosion-shaped granite blocks are thought to have been a religious focal point, possibly Neolithic or Bronze Age; no dig is recorded. Were burials made here?

row.old_value: A 12 m high tell with 5,000 years of stacked layers—Medieval, Roman, Iron Age, Bronze Age, and Copper Age. Each era is literally built on top of the last.
row.new_value: Tell Yunatsite rises 12 metres above modern ground level, holding the remains of at least 30 settlements, one over the other, left by peoples who settled here for more than 6,000 years.

row.old_value: Late 6th-century BC Greek rock tomb cut into a cliff above Wadi Taybsillu, visible for miles. Built for a high-ranking individual whose identity has been completely lost to history.
row.new_value: A late sixth-century BC Greek rock-tomb cut into a cliff near Marj, Al-Mnaykhrat is clearly visible across the plain. It was made for someone of high rank, yet no evidence tells us who.

row.old_value: A Mycenaean settlement that cultivated olives and terebinth for export during the Bronze Age. At its peak it had a royal-style megaron, though it was always smaller than Pylos.
row.new_value: On a ridgetop by the Messenian Gulf, Nichoria was a major outpost of Pylos and fell in the same event that claimed the palace there. At its acropolis foot, a burial circle held 7 people.

row.old_value: A 4.5-hectare mound 13 m high near Nal, occupied 3800–2300 BC. Its layered Togau, Kili Ghul Mohammad, and Kechi Beg pottery connects pre-Indus traditions to the Amri-Nal culture.
row.new_value: Near Nal in Balochistan, Sohr Damb, a mound 13 m high, holds a settlement of circa 3800–2300 BC that began before the Indus Valley Civilization, rich in cattle bones and bull figurines.

row.old_value: Maya site active 200 BC-1000 AD in northern Peten. La Joyanca sits east of La Florida (Namaan) near the border town of El Naranjo; its central area includes several temple-pyramids and other mounds.
row.new_value: Found in 1994 while an oil pipeline was being built, La Joyanca was a Maya city occupied for well over 1000 years, its vaulted Grupo Guacamaya possibly the palace of its rulers.

row.old_value: A fortified settlement dating to 7000 BC—one of the earliest walled sites known. It preserves the development of pre-Hassuna culture in Mesopotamia.
row.new_value: By the Abra River rises Tell Maghzaliyah, a fortified aceramic Mesolithic and Neolithic site whose deposits reach approximately 8 meters deep, with connections to the Jarmo culture.

row.old_value: Kingston Russell is the largest surviving stone circle in Dorset. The ring consists of eighteen stones, the longest of which are located at the north of the circle.
row.new_value: Kingston Russell Stone Circle, the largest surviving in Dorset, has never been excavated. In 1815 one of its stones still stood upright; by 1939 all of them lay on the ground.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age stone circle near Corfe Castle, hidden in dense woodland. Ten surviving gritstone boulders form an arc suggesting an original oval of ~26 m — Dorset's second-largest stone circle.
row.new_value: In a dense wood on the Isle of Purbeck remain the sandstone boulders of Rempstone Stone Circle, its southern half destroyed. In 1957 ploughing revealed a possible avenue leading to it.

row.old_value: Neolithic dolmen near St Keverne dated to 3300 BC, its two orthostats supporting a capstone with possible cup-mark depressions. The enclosed chamber measures roughly 4 by 2 m.
row.new_value: Near a hilltop overlooking Goonhilly Downs, upright stones hold the capstone of the Three Brothers of Grugith, a Neolithic dolmen; its hollows may be cup marks, or may be natural.

row.old_value: By the 4th century the villa was now a large courtyard villa enclosed on at least three sides.
row.new_value: A farmer digging out a ferret found Rockbourne Roman Villa in 1942. Two Roman milestones were reused in its fabric, and in 1967 a pottery jar yielded a hoard of 7717 bronze coins.

row.old_value: Poor Lot Barrow Cemetery is an archaeological site, a group of Bronze Age round barrows, near the A35 road about 2 miles west of Winterbourne Abbas, in Dorset.
row.new_value: Not on a ridge but on low-lying ground near the head of a valley lie the Bronze Age round barrows of Poor Lot Barrow Cemetery, from about 1500 BC. From a minor plateau, all can be seen.

row.old_value: Atella was a city of Oscan origin, one of the oldest in Campania and one of the first to have obtained the Roman civitas.
row.new_value: Atella, an Oscan city north of Naples, sided with Carthage after Cannae. Rome occupied it in 210 BC and executed its chief citizens, yet ruins of walls, houses and tombs remain.

row.old_value: Notgrove Long Barrow is a prehistoric long barrow burial mound in Gloucestershire.
row.new_value: In Gloucestershire, a passage runs through the heart of Notgrove Long Barrow to small chambers where human remains were laid. Open for thousands of years, it was sealed in 1976.

row.old_value: An Iron Age earthwork from 800 BC running for several kilometres. Linear earthworks like this marked tribal boundaries — not walls for defense, but lines of territorial claim.
row.new_value: Once thought a Roman road, Aves Ditch is an Iron Age boundary running about 3 miles through Oxfordshire that may have divided the Dobunni from the Catuvellauni. A skull lay in its ditch.

row.old_value: An oval stone circle of about 40 large pink granite stones, every single one now fallen. One lone limestone block sits among the granite — deliberately chosen to be different.
row.new_value: At the foot of Knott Hill in Cumbria, around 40 large stones of the Gamelands Stone Circle sit in a slight bank, an oval of 42 metres by 35 metres. Ploughing turned up two worked flints.

row.old_value: Roman practice camp earthworks and a hillfort share this plateau above Libanus in the Brecon Beacons. Rectangular outlines left by Roman military drills remain legible in the ground today.
row.new_value: Across the plateau of Mynydd Illtud the Roman road Sarn Helen can still be traced, while on the grassy mound of Twyn y Gaer an Iron Age hillfort overlooks the valley of the River Usk.

row.old_value: Five stone circles about 4,000 years old clustered on a hillside. The largest, Brat's Hill, has 42 stones forming an irregular ring 30 metres in diameter.
row.new_value: On the slopes of Boat How lie the Burnmoor Stone Circles, approximately 4,000 years old. In the largest, Brat's Hill, around 42 stones ring five funerary cairns and two further stones.
In the Shilikty Valley of eastern Kazakhstan, Early Saka kurgans held vast quantities of golden jewelry, and in 2003 the remains of a "golden man" were found with 4262 gold finds.

row.old_value: Wayna Tawqaray is situated at a height of about 3,600 metres on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray.
row.new_value: About 3,600 metres up on the slope of the mountain Tawqaray, above the river Watanay, lie the archaeological remains of Wayna Tawqaray, about 5 km southeast of the center of Cusco.

row.old_value: A Romano-Celtic temple discovered from cropmarks in 1959. Its rectangular plan with an inner cella follows the standard design of temples across Roman Britain.
row.new_value: Cropmarks gave away the Wicklewood Roman Temple in 1959: the walls of its inner chamber were painted in yellow and black on a red ground, and ornate brooches nearby suggest votive offerings.

row.old_value: A 1st-century AD Roman bridge on the road from Lisbon to Mérida. It wasn't identified as Roman until the 1980s despite being there for 2,000 years.
row.new_value: Near Sintra, the Roman Bridge of Catribana crosses the Bolelas stream in a single arch of local limestone. Close by lie traces of a Roman-era cemetery and a Neolithic settlement.

row.old_value: A double stone circle now completely destroyed. Built between 3300 and 900 BC, it was part of the megalithic tradition that spread across Britain, Ireland, and Brittany.
row.new_value: Fir Clump Stone Circle in Burderop Wood was a double oval ring of sarsen megaliths, levelled around the 1860s. Some rediscovered in 1965 were removed in 1969 during construction of the M4.
A farmer apparently took Kinniside Stone Circle apart for gate-posts in the 18th century. In 1925 its 11 granite stones were set in concrete, whether in their original holes is unclear.

row.old_value: Porth Hellick Down is a Neolithic and Bronze Age archeological site located on the island of St Mary's.
row.new_value: On St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, Porth Hellick Down holds at least six entrance graves. Unrecorded digs left the largest, The Great Tomb, empty but for pumice and a few potsherds.

row.old_value: Harappan site active 2600-1900 BC in Balochistan's Nasirabad District. A federally protected area between Jhat Pat and Dera Murad Jamali, occupied through the height of Indus civilisation.
row.new_value: Between Jhatpat and Dera Murad Jamali lie the remains of Judeir-jo-daro, a Harappan-period city in Balochistan once home to around 20,240 people, spread across 62 acres.

row.old_value: The circle, of the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age, is situated in a large clearing in the modern afforestation of Threestoneburn Wood, formerly overlooking a spacious valley to the east.
row.new_value: Threestoneburn Stone Circle sets 16 stones of local pink granite in a woodland clearing, four upright. A flint tool was found, and charcoal spreads that may be traces of fire-rituals.

row.old_value: Viracochapampa is located about 3.5 km north of Huamachuco in the region of La Libertad at an elevation of 3,070 metres.
row.new_value: Viracochapampa, its name possibly from the Andean divinity Wiracocha, holds a pre-Inca building complex at 3,070 metres: a Wari administrative center, occupied in the 7th and 8th centuries.

row.old_value: Inca tambo in the Junín highlands, part of the road-station network that linked the Inca empire's thousands of kilometres of road. Such way stations supplied travellers, armies, and state runners.
row.new_value: Its name possibly joins the Tarma, an ethnic group, with the Quechua word tampu, an inn: Tarmatambo, an archaeological site in the Junín Region, declared National Cultural Heritage in 2002.

row.old_value: The fort survives as earthworks, but no excavation of these has been carried out so far. With the rivers Eamont and Lowther flowing nearby and meeting to the west, the site had natural defences.
row.new_value: Brougham Castle sits on part of Brocavum, a Roman fort by the rivers Eamont and Lowther, and in its keep a Roman tombstone serves as a ceiling slab. The fort's earthworks remain unexcavated.

row.old_value: The Acropolis sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia, of unusual trapezoidal shape. It had no formal temple -- just an open precinct with a stoa to display offerings.
row.new_value: The Brauroneion, sanctuary of Artemis on the Athenian Acropolis, had no formal temple, only a stoa. Pausanias records an over-life-sized bronze horse there, representing the Trojan Horse.

row.old_value: At 15 meters tall, this is the largest tumulus on Rügen — the biggest of all prehistoric mounds on that island. Legend says a giant dropped a load of earth while trying to fill a nearby ford.
row.new_value: Local legend says a giant, carrying clay to fill a narrow ford, lost it on the way. Near Sagard it rises still: the Dobberworth, about 15 metres tall, the largest tumulus on Rügen.

row.old_value: The oldest known submerged city in the world, about 5,000 years old. It has a nearly complete town plan with streets, buildings, and tombs visible underwater.
row.new_value: In Vatika Bay, Pavlopetri keeps an almost complete town plan: at least 15 buildings lie in 3 to 4 metres of water, the town believed submerged by an earthquake around 1000 BCE.

row.old_value: The first formal archaeological excavation was carried out in 1955 by a team led by Hipólito Cabaço.
row.new_value: North of Lisbon, the Cave of Pedra Furada held a communal funeral space. Among the finds: flint arrowheads, beads, a polished stone axe and a bone figurine of a rabbit.

row.old_value: A 5.7-km linear earthwork that may date to the Bronze Age and was reactivated in the 4th century AD. A Roman road was cut through it, then the dyke was rebuilt across it.
row.new_value: Bokerley Dyke runs 5.75 kilometres across Cranborne Chase. Cut by a Roman road in the 1st century, it was remodelled in the 4th century and the road blocked, shortly after 364 AD.

row.old_value: Timber trackway from 2900–2500 BC, found in 2004 in a raised peat bog in the Humberhead Levels. Among the oldest ancient timber trackways known, preserved by centuries of waterlogged peat.
row.new_value: In October 2004 a local man walking the moors found worked wooden poles: the Hatfield Neolithic Trackway, one of the oldest known timber trackways in England, dating to around 2900–2500 BC.

row.old_value: A 2nd-century AD Iron Age fortification encircling 1,700 square meters on a hilltop. One side drops 70 meters into a ravine called the Devil's Valley.
row.new_value: Above the Devil's Valley, the Troldborg Ring guards a spring behind its circular rampart, likely a refuge in violent times. Its ash tells of massive fires whose source is unclear.

row.old_value: The gravesite was discovered in an olive grove near the ancient Palace of Nestor, within the Bronze Age city of Pylos.
row.new_value: In an olive grove near the Palace of Nestor, the Griffin Warrior Tomb held an intact skeleton and over 3500 items, among them the Pylos Combat Agate and four signet gold rings.

row.old_value: Ruins of a Roman bridge built around 90 AD to carry Dere Street over the River Tees. The river has since shifted 90 metres, leaving the bridge stranded in a field.
row.new_value: Gravel quarrying in 1972 uncovered massive masonry blocks by the River Tees: Piercebridge Roman Bridge, which once carried Dere Street across the river, guarded by a Roman fort.

row.old_value: Two 1st-century Roman marching camps flanking Dere Street, the military road from York into Scotland. Troops camped here during campaigns against northern tribes.
row.new_value: Beside Dere Street, a Roman road running into Scotland, the Featherwood Roman Camps lie about 500 metres apart, two Roman camps that are now scheduled monuments.

Passing an infant through one of its natural holes was believed to cure measles and whooping cough: the Longstone of Minchinhampton, a large piece of oolitic limestone 7.5 feet high.

row.old_value: A downland spur in Wiltshire holds an enclosed Iron Age settlement and field system; the outer enclosure measures 700 by 400 metres. Roman-era layers sit above, preserving two superimposed cultures.
row.new_value: Banks reinforce the downland spur of Ebsbury, a possible hill fort. Buried in two earthenware pots lay Roman coins from between AD 337 and AD 408, found with six silver rings.

row.old_value: A 3 km Neolithic earthwork from 3630–3375 BC—centuries before Stonehenge itself. It was the first monument built in this vast ritual landscape.
row.new_value: A red deer antler pick from its ditch suggests the Stonehenge Cursus was first built between 3630 and 3375 BCE. Just under 3 km long, it is oriented toward the equinox sunrise.

row.old_value: A Neolithic burial cairn 45 metres long with a single chamber of upright slabs capped by lintels. The chamber inside measured 4.5 metres long but less than a metre wide and high.
row.new_value: On a ridge of Anglezarke moor lie five large gritstone slabs, remains of the burial chamber of Pikestones, a Neolithic cairn once covered by a huge mound of stones and turves.

row.old_value: A Neolithic dolmen with three uprights supporting a robust wedge-shaped capstone. A large flat stone nearby may be the collapsed remains of the original structure.
row.new_value: In a farmer's field on Anglesey, three upright stones of Bodowyr Burial Chamber hold up a robust, wedge-shaped capstone. In 1833 four were said to hold it: one seems to have fallen since.

row.old_value: Late Neolithic burial chamber built between 4500 and 2000 BC. Its local name — anta — belongs to a tradition of roughly 5,000 megalithic tombs constructed across the region during the Neolithic.
row.new_value: The Late Neolithic Anta das Pedras Grandes is the only surviving dolmen in its immediate area. Around it lay many flint chippings, suggesting that flint items were once made here.

row.old_value: This Dere Street fort in County Durham was garrisoned by the Twentieth Legion. An inscription slab naming them was later reused as building material — history recycled by soldiers.
row.new_value: On high ground by Dere Street, the Roman fort of Longovicium drew water from two aqueducts, one fed by a stone-faced dam that harnessed 21 springs and stood 20 feet high.

row.old_value: Pons Aelius was a fort and Roman settlement at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, at the site now occupied by The Castle, Newcastle.
row.new_value: Beneath the medieval Castle Keep that gave Newcastle its name lies much of Pons Aelius, a Roman fort whose name means Aelian Bridge, at the original eastern end of Hadrian's Wall.

row.old_value: Three standing stones up to 6.9 meters tall, grooved by millennia of rainfall. Originally more existed — a fourth was re-erected in 1903 to improve the skyline.
row.new_value: Grooved by millennia of rainfall, the three Devil's Arrows stand in an almost straight line outside Boroughbridge. The tallest reaches 22.5 feet; the stones came from Brimham Rocks.

row.old_value: A site along the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road system that stretched over 30,000 km across the Andes. Way stations like this kept the empire's relay messengers running.
row.new_value: Along a section of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system, lies Maray Qalla in Peru's Ancash Region. In Quechua, maray can mean grindstone and qalla carved stone or cobblestone.
On Dorset's chalk uplands, the large multivallate hillfort of Eggardon Hill encloses approximately 21ha. Older Bronze Age earthworks cross its interior, and two bowl barrows lie within.

54 km southeast of Puno in the Titicaca Basin, Jisk'a Iru Muqu was occupied from circa 3400-1600 BCE. Excavations recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace and early domestic architecture.
A Roman road ran from Poetovio in the north to Siscia in the south, and Pyrri stood along it in Pannonia. Evidence suggests the settlement lies under the village of Komin today.
Seven Barrows is a Bronze Age barrow cemetery at Upper Lambourn in Berkshire, England. Its unimproved chalk grassland supports over 100 herb species and a rich insect fauna.
Near Porodin, near Bitola, the Neolithic settlement of Veluška Tumba is a raised mound shaped like a truncated cone, 250 m long and 150 m wide, holding a cultural layer four metres thick.
Near Southleigh in Devon, the Iron Age hillfort of Blackbury Camp encloses roughly 200 m by 100 m behind a rampart about 3 m high, and excavations uncovered over 1,000 slingstones.
In a private front garden on the Islandmagee peninsula stands Ballylumford Dolmen, known locally as the Druid's Altar: four upright stones under a heavy capstone, and a fallen stone inside.
Drusus founded the Ara trium Galliarum at Lugdunum, where the Rhone and Saone meet, as a sanctuary to Roma and Augustus. Its altar bore the names of 60 Gallic tribes.

row.old_value: 54 km southeast of Puno in the Titicaca Basin, Jisk'a Iru Muqu was occupied from circa 3400-1600 BCE. Excavations recovered obsidian tools, a gold necklace and early domestic architecture.
A Roman road ran from Poetovio in the north to Siscia in the south, and Pyrri stood along it in Pannonia. Evidence suggests the settlement lies under the village of Komin today.
In a private front garden on the Islandmagee peninsula stands Ballylumford Dolmen, known locally as the Druid's Altar: four upright stones under a heavy capstone, and a fallen stone inside.
